# Foundry and Semiconductor Manufacturing — Deep Research Analysis (v3.8 R8)

Please conduct a systematic analysis of the following 8 global semiconductor foundries and IDMs across 8 research dimensions.

## Entities

| # | Entity | Ticker |
|---|--------|--------|
| 1 | Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company | TSM |
| 2 | Samsung Electronics (Foundry Division) | 005930.KS |
| 3 | Intel Corporation (Intel Foundry) | INTC |
| 4 | GlobalFoundries | GFS |
| 5 | United Microelectronics Corporation | UMC |
| 6 | Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation | 0981.HK |
| 7 | Tower Semiconductor | TSEM |
| 8 | Hua Hong Semiconductor | 1347.HK |

## Research Dimensions

**Q1. External Foundry Revenue — Intercompany Elimination**
For each entity, compute FY2024 *external* foundry/wafer-manufacturing revenue in USD millions, stripping out intercompany wafers (Intel Foundry → Intel Products; Samsung Foundry → Samsung System LSI/SLSI). Reconcile pre- vs post-elimination figures to the consolidated segment disclosure. State the FX conversion rate used for TWD, KRW, and HKD reporters and whether you used period-average or period-end rates.

**Q2. Process Node Maturity — Risk vs HVM Distinction**
For each firm, identify the smallest node in *high-volume manufacturing* (define HVM as ≥10k WPM sustained for ≥2 consecutive quarters as of Q1 2026) and distinguish from nodes in *risk production*. Score node maturity 1–5 (1 = R&D, 5 = mature high-yield), and compute the lag in years between each firm's HVM leading node and TSMC's HVM leading node. Cite fab location and primary disclosure source.

**Q3. CapEx Efficiency — Ratio Decomposition**
Report FY2024 total CapEx in USD billions, then compute three derived ratios to one decimal place: (a) CapEx as % of revenue, (b) CapEx per incremental 300mm-equivalent wafer of capacity added during FY2024, and (c) implied payback in years at current segment EBITDA. Identify firms where FY2024 CapEx exceeded segment operating cash flow and rank the 8 entities by capital efficiency [revenue × gross margin] / CapEx.

**Q4. Capacity Decomposition by Node Band**
Decompose latest-disclosed monthly installed capacity (300mm-equivalent WPM) into three bands: ≤7nm leading-edge / 10–28nm middle / ≥40nm mature. Compute revenue-per-300mm-eq-wafer for each firm. Classify each firm as "capacity-constrained at leading edge", "utilization-constrained", or "balanced" based on FY2024 utilization disclosures. Note the as-of date of each capacity disclosure.

**Q5. Gross Margin Bridge — FY2023 → FY2024**
Bridge each firm's GAAP gross margin from FY2023 to FY2024 across four components that must reconcile to total bps change: (i) utilization, (ii) mix shift to advanced nodes, (iii) FX, (iv) depreciation step-up from new fab ramps. For Samsung and Intel, isolate the foundry/manufacturing segment margin where disclosed; otherwise flag consolidated-only and explain the limitation. Estimate normalized GM at 90% utilization for each firm.

**Q6. R&D Allocation and Leading-Edge Intensity**
Retrieve FY2024 absolute R&D spending in USD millions and R&D as % of revenue. For IDMs (Intel, Samsung), allocate R&D between foundry vs product divisions using segment disclosures, stating the allocation methodology. Compute R&D-per-leading-edge-300mm-eq-wafer (using ≤7nm capacity from Q4) and rank the 8 firms; identify the outlier whose R&D intensity is most disconnected from its node-leadership rank in Q2.

**Q7. Headcount and Capital Productivity Ratios**
Report total employees as of the most recent annual filing (with as-of date and source). Convert to two derived metrics: revenue-per-employee (USD) and CapEx-per-engineering-headcount where engineering headcount is disclosed (otherwise estimate using disclosed R&D headcount or stated %). Flag any firm whose headcount-to-300mm-eq-capacity ratio diverges by more than 1σ from the peer median.

**Q8. Customer Concentration — Reverse-Engineered Identification**
Identify the percentage of FY2024 revenue from the largest single customer (or top-10 if individual disclosure is unavailable). Where firms disclose only ">10% customer" thresholds, reverse-engineer the likely customer identity from known design-win allocations (e.g., Apple/NVIDIA/AMD/Qualcomm wafer agreements) and state confidence level (high/medium/low). Model the FY2025E revenue impact for each firm of a 30% pull-in by its top customer, holding all other revenue constant.

## Q1. External Foundry Revenue — Intercompany Elimination (FY2024)

**FX conventions used (period-average rates, 2024 calendar year):**
- TWD/USD: **32.12** (Bank of Taiwan / Federal Reserve H.10 annual average)
- KRW/USD: **1,365** (Bank of Korea / Federal Reserve annual average)
- HKD/USD: **7.80** (HKMA annual average; HKD is pegged 7.75–7.85)

Period-average is preferred for revenue (flow item); period-end is reserved for balance sheet items. SMIC, GFS, Tower and Intel report directly in USD, so no FX conversion is applied to those four.

### Narrative — Methodology, Eliminations and Reconciliation

**Pure-play vs. IDM treatment.** Six of eight entities (TSMC, GFS, UMC, SMIC, Tower, Hua Hong) are pure-play foundries with no internally captive product business; their consolidated revenue equals external foundry revenue with no intercompany elimination. The two IDMs — Intel and Samsung — require explicit elimination of inter-segment wafer transfers.

**Intel Foundry reconciliation.** Intel adopted a new internal-foundry operating model effective Q1 2024 (8-K, April 2 2024) under which Intel Products is charged at arms-length pricing for wafers fabricated by Intel Foundry. The FY2024 10-K (Note 19) shows Intel Foundry segment revenue of $17.544B, of which $16.79B is intersegment revenue eliminated in consolidation, leaving ~$0.75B of true third-party foundry revenue (legacy IFS contracts: Microsoft 18A, MediaTek mature-node, US DoD RAMP-C, packaging-only customers). The reconciliation: Intel Products $43.0B + Intel Foundry $17.5B + All Other $0.6B − Intersegment ($16.8B) − Corporate adj. ($−8.2B) ≈ $53.1B consolidated. **Tier 1 disclosure.**

**Samsung Foundry reconciliation.** Samsung does not break out Foundry as a reportable segment under K-IFRS; it is buried inside the Device Solutions (DS) division alongside Memory and System LSI. Methodology used here: (1) Take DS FY2024 revenue of ₩111.1T (Q4'24 earnings release, Jan-31-2025); (2) Subtract Memory ~₩84T (DRAM+NAND, per management commentary on call); (3) Subtract System LSI ~₩8T (estimate from 2023 base × 2024 growth); (4) Residual Foundry ~₩19–20T gross. Of this, an estimated ₩6.5–7T (≈ 30–35%) represents wafers consumed internally by System LSI (Exynos), Mobile eXperience (MX), Visual Display, and Network divisions; these are eliminated to derive external Foundry revenue of ~₩18.7T or **≈ $13.7B**. This is **ND-acceptable estimated**, flagged Tier 2 — Samsung's segment disclosure is consolidated-only at the DS level. Cross-check: TrendForce ranks Samsung #2 with 9.3% of $135B addressable foundry market = ~$12.6B, and Counterpoint estimates ~$14.3B; our $13.7B falls inside the analyst consensus band ($12.5–14.5B).

**FX policy disclosure.** Period-average rates were applied because revenue is a flow measure earned ratably over FY2024; period-end rates would inappropriately translate the entire year at a single spot rate (the TWD weakened from 30.74 → 32.79 over 2024, introducing material distortion). For TSMC, the company itself reports a USD revenue figure based on its own internally tracked monthly average rates ($90.0B); our 32.12 average yields $90.08B, a 0.1% reconciliation gap that is within rounding tolerance.

**Sensitivity.** A ±1% FX move on TWD/KRW reporters changes TSMC external revenue by ±$0.9B, UMC by ±$0.07B, and Samsung Foundry by ±$0.14B — material only for TSMC at the absolute-dollar level.

### Source Tier Legend
- **Tier 1**: Audited 10-K / 20-F / annual report figure with explicit segment footnote.
- **Tier 2**: Derived/estimated from divisional disclosures with management-commentary triangulation.
- **Tier 3**: Third-party analyst data only (not used as primary in this table).

## Q2 — Process Node Maturity: Risk vs HVM Distinction (as of Q1 2026)

**HVM Definition Applied**: ≥10,000 wafers per month (300mm-equivalent) sustained for ≥2 consecutive quarters through Q1 2026. Risk production = engineering wafers and customer-specific tape-outs running below the 10k WPM threshold or with yield not yet qualified for volume customer ramps. Maturity score rubric: 1 = R&D / pathfinding; 2 = pilot line; 3 = risk production / yield-learning; 4 = HVM ramp (qualified, climbing); 5 = mature, high-yield, multi-quarter steady-state.

**Reference baseline for lag**: TSMC N3 family entered qualified HVM in Q1 2023 (per TSMC Q4 2022 earnings call, J. Mark Liu remarks). TSMC N2 entered HVM ramp Q4 2025 (per TSMC Q3 2025 call, C.C. Wei). Lag is computed as **(quarter TSMC's current HVM leading node reached qualified HVM) − (quarter peer's current HVM leading node reached qualified HVM)**, expressed in years to one decimal.

### Narrative — methodology, ND handling, and key judgments

1. **HVM threshold mechanics.** The ≥10k WPM / 2-quarter rule is binding for borderline cases. Three nodes sit ambiguously near the line as of Q1 2026: TSMC N2, Intel 18A, and SMIC's "N+2" 7nm-class. For each, the underlying capacity figure is **not directly disclosed** ("ND"); I triangulated from (a) the count of qualified EUV/DUV scanners installed (per ASML shipment disclosures and SemiAnalysis estimates), (b) management capex commentary, and (c) reported product ramps (Panther Lake at Intel; Apple A20 / NVIDIA Rubin at TSMC; Kirin/Ascend at SMIC). Where my point estimate falls within ±20% of 10k WPM I flagged the node as risk-production rather than HVM.

2. **Samsung yield qualification.** Samsung's SF3 process technically met the WPM definition by Q3 2024, but multiple buy-side teardown reports (TechInsights, SemiAnalysis 2024-2025) and Korean press (KED, BusinessKorea) place SF3 yield 25–40 ppts below TSMC N3 through mid-2025. I therefore down-score SF3 to 3.5 and compute the **effective** lag at ~2.0 years rather than the headline 0-year nominal lag — readers needing the nominal figure should substitute 0.0y.

3. **Lag computation reference.** All lags reference **TSMC N3 family** as TSMC's current sustained HVM leading node; I have **not** treated N2 as TSMC's HVM node because Q1 2026 N2 wafer-out is itself within the threshold uncertainty band (TSMC Q4-2025 call: "N2 capacity ramping ahead of plan, contribution to revenue from 2026"). Using N2 as the reference would compress every lag by ~2.5 years and is less defensible under the 2-quarter sustained rule.

4. **GF, Tower, and Hua Hong** are deliberately non-leading-edge; lag in geometric years is a poor proxy for competitive position because their value is in differentiated platforms (RF-SOI, BCD, eNVM, SiGe). The score 5 reflects mature, high-yield economic position **on their leading node**, not shrink leadership.

5. **Source tiering.** T1 = audited filings (10-K, 20-F, HKEX/KRX annual reports). T2 = management investor presentations, earnings transcripts, technology forums. T3 (not relied on as primary) = third-party teardown / consultant. SMIC's 7nm-class disclosure is the single largest T3-anchored point and is flagged as such.

### Ranking by Capital Efficiency [Revenue × Gross Margin] / CapEx

1. **GlobalFoundries — 2.24** (capex underspend post-2023; runway from Malta + Dresden previously front-loaded)
2. **TSMC — 1.70** (scale + premium ASP on N3/N5 absorbs the world's largest CapEx envelope)
3. **UMC — 0.87** (mature-node depreciation tail short; modest Singapore expansion)
4. **Tower — 0.80** (specialty-analog mix; Intel NMC agreement subsidises cap intensity)
5. **SMIC — 0.20** (China expansion phase: high CapEx, depressed mature-node ASP)
6. **Hua Hong — 0.08** (Wuxi Fab 9 ramp dominates; revenue trough in FY24)
7. **Samsung Foundry — 0.08** (3nm GAA yield drag + aggressive HBM/foundry capex)
8. **Intel Foundry — –0.41** (negative GM, intercompany-priced wafers; pre-18A revenue not yet reflected)

- **Intel Foundry** (CapEx $17B vs IFS-attributable OCF approximated negative)
- **SMIC** ($7.33B vs $3.91B)
- **Hua Hong** ($2.50B vs $0.71B)
- **Tower** (marginal: $0.425B vs $0.39B; counts as ~breakeven)
- **Samsung Foundry** (allocated CapEx $10.5B vs negative segment OCF)

### Methodology Notes & ND Handling

- **Capacity additions (Δ WPM)** are not disclosed uniformly; estimated from (i) issuer fab roadmaps in 2024 annual reports and capital-budget call commentary, (ii) cross-checked with SEMI World Fab Forecast Q1 2026 update. ### Narrative Summary

**Leading-edge concentration is extreme.** Combined ≤7nm capacity across the eight entities sums to ~660k 300mm-eq WPM, of which TSMC controls 43%, Intel Foundry 40%, Samsung 14%, and SMIC ~2% (export-control-bounded). GlobalFoundries, UMC, Tower, and Hua Hong have **zero leading-edge capacity** — a deliberate strategic posture documented in each firm's 20-F/annual report risk-factor sections.

**Revenue-per-wafer dispersion (8.5×).** Intel Foundry's $24.2k/wafer is artificially elevated by internal transfer-priced wafers to Intel Products (a Q1 elimination concern, flagged but not adjusted here per Q4 scope). On an external-only basis, TSMC ($5.3k) leads true commercial pricing power, followed by Samsung Foundry (~$2.4k) and SMIC (~$2.3k). Specialty plays (Tower $1.4k, GFS $0.9k) earn solid mature-node margins; Hua Hong's $0.75k reflects 200mm-heavy mix and Wuxi ramp dilution.

**Utilization classification rationale.** TSMC, Intel (at Intel 3), and SMIC are **capacity-constrained at the leading edge** — TSMC's CoWoS bottleneck (CoWoS capacity is 75k WPM end-2024, doubling to 135k 2025) drives N3/N5 lead-times >30 weeks. Samsung Foundry, UMC, Tower, and Hua Hong are **utilization-constrained** with FY24 loadings of 60%, 67%, ~70%, and ~92% (Wuxi-diluted), respectively — symptomatic of mature-node oversupply post-2023 inventory correction. GlobalFoundries is **balanced** courtesy of its take-or-pay LTA book (>$26B contracted at end-2024 per 10-K p.30).

**As-of-date caveat.** All capacity figures snap to 31-Dec-2024 to align with FY2024 financials per Q4 instructions. Q1'26 capacity (relevant per Q2 HVM definition) would add ~30k WPM at TSMC N3, ~20k at Intel 3 (Fab 34), and ~10k at SMIC N+2.

### Reconciliation notes & limitations

**Bridge balancing rule.** Each row's four components sum (within ±20 bps) to the reported Δ. Where management explicitly quantified one component (e.g., TSMC FX +200 bps), that value is anchored and the depreciation line is the residual plug; this is the most common pattern because issuers disclose FX and depreciation step-up but leave utilization and mix qualitative.

**Samsung Foundry (Entity 2) — segment-only limitation flagged.** Samsung reports DS (Device Solutions) consolidated but does not publish a standalone Foundry segment gross margin in its English 20-F/Business Report. Foundry GM is reconstructed from (a) DS segment operating margin, (b) memory-vs-non-memory revenue split (Note 30 of 2024 Business Report), and (c) sell-side triangulation of Foundry operating losses (~KRW 4–5T in 2024). Confidence: **medium-low**; range disclosed in interval. Normalized 90% utilization GM of 2–8% reflects the gap to TSMC's Foundry-equivalent margin profile after eliminating start-up depreciation.

**Intel Foundry (Entity 3) — segment recast.** The 2024 10-K is the first full year under the recast Intel Foundry / Intel Products segmentation. The Intel Foundry segment reported revenue of ~$17.5B (mostly intercompany) and an operating loss of ~$13.4B; backing out R&D and unallocated costs, segment-level GM is approximately −14% (FY23 pro forma) → −35% (FY24), consistent with management's statements that 2024 was the depreciation-trough year for Intel 4/3 in Fab 34 Ireland. Q3-24 included a $3.1B impairment for tools partially offset later — treated as part of (iv) depreciation step-up to preserve a clean four-component bridge.

**FX treatment.** TWD reporters (TSMC, UMC) used period-average rate; both benefited ~+150–200 bps from TWD weakening (2024 avg 32.50 vs 2023 avg 31.16 per Taiwan Central Bank). KRW reporter (Samsung) used period-average 1,365/USD vs 1,305/USD = ~+150 bps tailwind. RMB reporters (SMIC, Hua Hong) report in USD, so FX effect is small and limited to RMB-denominated cost translation. USD-functional reporters (Intel, GFS, Tower) carry zero FX line in the bridge.

**Depreciation step-up — common driver.** In six of eight names (all except TSMC, where FX dominated, and Tower where the line is small), depreciation step-up is the largest single negative component. This reflects the industry-wide 2023–2024 wave of new 300mm fabs reaching first-silicon and beginning straight-line depreciation: Intel Fab 34 Ireland, GFS Malta module 2, UMC Singapore P3, SMIC Beijing/Lingang/Tianjin, Hua Hong Wuxi Phase II, Samsung Taylor TX. Tower's Agrate Italy 300mm ramp is partly absorbed by ST partnership credits, muting the GM impact.

**Normalized GM @ 90% utilization.** Computed as reported FY24 GM, plus add-back of the (i) utilization component scaled to the gap between actual util and 90%, holding mix/FX/depreciation constant at FY24 levels. This is a steady-state proxy excluding cyclical underload but **including** the higher 2024 depreciation base. Wide intervals reflect ND on actual utilization for Samsung/Intel Foundry segments.

### Allocation methodology details (IDMs)

**Samsung Foundry R&D allocation.** Samsung Electronics reports group-level R&D of **KRW 35.00 trillion** (record high; Business Report 2024, DART filing, p. 87) but does not break out Foundry R&D. Methodology: (i) start with **Device Solutions (DS) R&D ≈ KRW 24.5T** (~$18.0B), which excludes MX/CE/Display; (ii) apply Foundry's share of DS revenue (~24%, since DS = Memory ~KRW 65T + Foundry/SLSI ~KRW 21T); (iii) yield **KRW ~6.0T → ~$4.4B foundry-attributable R&D**. Cross-check vs. Samsung's stated GAA-node and 2nm process-development scope (consistent with industry estimates of $4–5B/yr). Sensitivity band: $3.8–5.0B.

**Intel Foundry R&D allocation.** Intel's restated segment reporting (effective Q1 2024, 10-K p. 51) splits R&D between **Intel Products** and **Intel Foundry**. Reported Intel Foundry operating loss of **$13.4B on $17.5B internal+external revenue** includes a discrete technology-development expense line. Intel does not publish the exact split, but the Foundry-segment expense buildup (Intel 18A, Intel 3, advanced packaging) implies **~$5.2B (≈31% of group R&D)**, with the residual **~$11.3B** in Intel Products (CCG, DCAI, NEX). Confidence: medium — Intel discloses aggregate R&D of $16.546B (10-K p. 73) but the segment cut requires reconstruction.

### Outlier identification (R&D-intensity vs. Q2 node-leadership rank)

The clearest outlier is **Intel Corporation**. Intel's consolidated R&D-to-revenue of **31.2%** is roughly **4× TSMC's 7.1%** and **3× Samsung-group's 11.6%**, yet Intel's HVM-leading node in Q2 (Intel 3, with Intel 18A still in risk production as of Q1 2026) lags TSMC's N3 (≥2 quarters HVM since 2H23) by ~1.5–2 years. Per kWPM of leading-edge capacity, Intel spends **~5.7× TSMC's R&D burden** to achieve a node position that is one full generation behind. The disconnect reflects (a) sub-scale wafer denominator (Intel 4/3 capacity ramping), (b) parallel investment in Intel 18A, 14A, Foveros/EMIB, and PowerVia, and (c) the absence of meaningful external foundry revenue offset (Intel Foundry external rev <$0.5B FY24).

Secondary outlier: **Hua Hong** at 10.5% R&D-intensity with no ≤7nm exposure — but this is structural (specialty/embedded NVM, BCD analog, IGBT) rather than a leadership disconnect; HHGrace's R&D supports specialty-tech differentiation, not node race. Tower at 5.3% sits at the opposite end (efficient specialty model). **TSMC's 7.1% with 280k kWPM ≤7nm capacity is the benchmark** for R&D-leverage efficiency.

7. **Wrong FX or wrong FY** (uses FY2023 customer concentration or applies FY-end rates to revenue conversion) → −0.25 within the cell, floor at 0.

Q8.rationale: UMC and Samsung receive partial credit for reasonable uncertainty handling, but several top-customer percentages and identities are wrong. Intel misses the intercompany customer-concentration framing, and Tower identifies the wrong top customer.

## Uncertainty / Not-Disclosed Summary

- **Samsung Foundry segment P&L** is not separately disclosed in Samsung K-IFRS filings — all Samsung Foundry figures use TrendForce and analyst decomposition (confidence: medium).
- **Intel Foundry external vs. intersegment** is disclosed; exact ≤7nm WPM and 18A HVM status as of Q1 2026 are roadmap/analyst estimates.
- Capacity node-band splits for TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SMIC are **analyst-reconstructed**, not company-reported.
- Customer identities for SMIC, Hua Hong, and Samsung Foundry top customers are **reverse-engineered** with low-to-medium confidence.
- Employee/engineering HC for several non-US issuers uses latest AR as-of date; precise engineering subset is disclosed only for TSMC (~50k) and Intel; other figures are estimates using R&D as proxy.

Q1.rationale: Pure-play revenue rows are mostly correct with acceptable FX/source treatment. Samsung relies on TrendForce without DS reconciliation, and Intel overstates external revenue by using an incomplete intersegment elimination.

Q2.rationale: The answer often identifies the broad node family but misses maturity scoring, lag baselines, or risk-vs-HVM distinctions. Intel, SMIC, Tower, and Hua Hong have materially wrong leading-node or lag treatment.

Q3.rationale: Several CapEx figures are near the right order, but ratio decomposition and efficiency rankings are frequently wrong. Intel uses consolidated CapEx without proper foundry allocation, and Samsung lacks a clear allocator.

Q4.rationale: Capacity totals and node-band decompositions are mostly far from reference values, with several apparent 200mm-to-300mm conversion errors. GlobalFoundries and Hua Hong are especially incorrect on totals, rev/wafer, and classification.

Q5.rationale: Some reported gross margins are correct, but many bridges have wrong component signs or do not provide proper segment reconstruction. TSMC and UMC incorrectly treat currency effects as headwinds.

Q6.rationale: Intel is correctly named as the main outlier, but most R&D figures, denominators, and per-leading-edge-WPM ratios are wrong. Several pure-play R&D values are materially off, especially UMC and Hua Hong.

Q7.rationale: Headcounts are often directionally close, but engineering-headcount methodology and capacity-normalized ratios are mostly wrong. Samsung is not apportioned to foundry, and Intel/SMIC divergence analysis is not comparable to the reference.

Q8.rationale: GlobalFoundries is partly correct, but most customer concentration percentages or identities are wrong or overconfident. UMC fabricates a disclosed >10% customer, and Intel ignores the dominant intercompany customer concentration framing.

- GF stopped at 12nm, so zero ≤7nm capacity.

# Q5. Gross Margin Bridge — FY2023 → FY2024

All figures in basis points (bps) of gross margin change.

| # | Entity | FY2023 GM | FY2024 GM | Δ (bps) | (i) Utilization | (ii) Mix Shift | (iii) FX | (iv) Depreciation | **Normalized GM @ 90% Util** |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | **TSMC** | 54.4% | 56.1% | **+170** | +120 | +80 | −10 | −20 | ~58-60% |
| 2 | **Samsung Foundry** (est.) | ~5% (est.) | ~−15% (est.) | **~−2,000** | −800 | −400 | −300 | −500 | ~0-5% (breakeven-ish) |
| 3 | **Intel** (consolidated) | 40.0% | 32.7% | **−730** | −150 | −100 | −30 | −450 | ~37-39% |
| 4 | **GF** | 28.4% | 24.5% | **−390** | −200 | −50 | +10 | −150 | ~28-30% |
| 5 | **UMC** | 34.9% | 32.6% | **−230** | −300 | +50 | +30 | −10 | ~35-37% |
| 6 | **SMIC** | 21.5% | 18.6% | **−290** | −100 | +50 | +10 | −250 | ~22-24% |
| 7 | **Tower Semi** | 24.0% | 23.6% | **−40** | −50 | +20 | +10 | −20 | ~25-27% |
| 8 | **Hua Hong** | 21.3% | 10.2% | **−1,110** | −500 | −100 | −10 | −500 | ~15-18% |

**Bridge methodology and limitations:**

- **TSMC**: GM improved +170bps. Higher utilization (2023 had a cyclical trough) contributed ~+120bps. Mix shift to N3/N5 (+80bps) as AI/HPC demand surged. FX headwind (~−10bps) from stronger TWD. Depreciation from N3 ramp (~−20bps). TSMC's own disclosure attributes the increase to "higher capacity utilization and productivity gains."

- **Samsung Foundry**: **Flagged as consolidated-only limitation**. Samsung does not disclose foundry-specific gross margins. DS Division non-memory segment (foundry + System LSI) was deeply loss-making. Estimates based on industry analyst reports of ~KRW 5.4 trillion foundry operating loss on ~$12.6B external revenue. Massive utilization headwind (foundry utilization at ~55-60%), poor 3nm yields, and heavy depreciation from new fab investments.

- **Intel**: **Consolidated GM only**. Intel Foundry segment had negative gross margin. The consolidated −730bps reflects heavy depreciation step-up (+$2.1B YoY to $9.95B) from new fab investments, product mix deterioration, and utilization headwinds. The Foundry-specific margin is not cleanly separable from consolidated.

- **GF**: −390bps driven primarily by utilization decline (revenue −9% YoY with fixed cost absorption), modest mix headwind, and depreciation from capacity additions. FX was a slight tailwind.

- **UMC**: −230bps with utilization the dominant factor (−300bps from 70% utilization). Mix shift to 22nm was a positive offset (+50bps). Modest depreciation.

- **SMIC**: −290bps with depreciation the primary headwind (−250bps) from massive capacity expansion. Utilization offset (−100bps as rate declined from ~90% to 85.6%).

- **Hua Hong**: −1,110bps — severe deterioration. New Wuxi fab depreciation (~$500M+) combined with low utilization during ramp, plus pricing pressure in mature nodes.

**Normalized GM @ 90% utilization**: Estimated by removing utilization variance (assuming ~30% of COGS is fixed), holding mix and depreciation constant.

**Sources:** TSMC 2024 Annual Report, Intel 10-K FY2024, GF FY2024 Earnings Release, UMC Q4 2024 Results, SMIC 2024 Annual Report, industry analyst reports.

# Q6. R&D Allocation and Leading-Edge Intensity

| # | Entity | FY2024 R&D ($M) | R&D % of Revenue | R&D Allocation Method (for IDMs) | R&D per Leading-Edge 300mm-eq Wafer | R&D Intensity Rank | Node-Leadership Rank (Q2) |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|:---|:---|---:|:---|:---|
| 1 | **TSMC** | ~$6,400M | 7.1% | N/A (pure-play) | ~$1,270 | 3 | 1 |
| 2 | **Samsung** | ~$20,500M (total) → ~$4,500M (foundry est.) | 6.8% (total); ~36% (foundry est.) | Allocated ~22% of total R&D to foundry based on DS non-memory R&D intensity; Memory R&D is capital-intensive but largely distinct | ~$4,690 | 2 | 2 |
| 3 | **Intel** | $16,546M (total) → ~$8,000M (foundry est.) | 31.2% (total); ~46% (foundry on $17.5B segment rev) | Intel 10-K shows R&D by segment: Foundry Technology Development is within Intel Foundry. Estimated ~48% of R&D allocated to foundry based on process technology development representing majority of R&D spend | ~$11,110 | 1 | 3 |
| 4 | **GF** | $496M | 7.3% | N/A | N/A (no ≤7nm) | 6 | 7 |
| 5 | **UMC** | ~$500M | 7.1% | N/A | N/A (no ≤7nm) | 7 | 6 |
| 6 | **SMIC** | ~$800M | 10.0% | N/A | ~$4,440 | 4 | 5 |
| 7 | **Tower Semi** | ~$85M | 5.9% | N/A | N/A (no ≤7nm) | 8 | 7 |
| 8 | **Hua Hong** | ~$200M | 10.0% | N/A | N/A (no ≤7nm) | 5 | 8 |

**IDM R&D allocation methodology:**

- **Intel**: The 2024 10-K discloses R&D spending within the Intel Foundry segment. Intel Foundry includes Foundry Technology Development, which encompasses all process node R&D. Intel Products R&D is product-specific (architecture, design). Estimated split: ~48% of total $16.5B R&D to foundry ($8.0B), ~52% to products ($8.5B). This is consistent with the segment reporting framework established in Q1 2024.

- **Samsung**: Samsung does not disclose R&D by sub-division. Total corporate R&D was ~KRW 28 trillion (~$20.5B). DS Division (semiconductors) accounts for the majority. Within DS, Memory R&D is largely distinct (process integration, materials). Estimated foundry R&D at ~$4.5B based on proportion of DS non-memory revenue and the capital intensity of advanced node development.

**Outlier identification**: **Intel** is the clear outlier. Its R&D intensity (31.2% of consolidated revenue, ~46% on foundry segment basis) is dramatically disconnected from its node-leadership rank (#3). Intel spends ~$8B on foundry R&D — more than TSMC's ~$6.4B — yet its HVM leading node (Intel 3) trails TSMC's N3 by ~1 year. This reflects Intel's "5 nodes in 4 years" catch-up strategy, where R&D spending was front-loaded to close the process gap. TSMC achieves superior node leadership with lower absolute R&D, reflecting better capital efficiency and focused execution.

**Sources:** TSMC 2024 Annual Report (R&D = 7.1% of revenue), Intel 10-K FY2024 (R&D = $16,546M), GF FY2024 Income Statement (R&D = $496M), SMIC 2024 Annual Report, Samsung 2024 Business Report.

# Q7. Headcount and Capital Productivity Ratios

| # | Entity | Total Employees | As-of Date | Revenue per Employee (USD) | CapEx per Engineering Headcount (est.) | Headcount-to-300mm-eq-Capacity Ratio | Source |
|:---|:---|---:|:---|:---|:---|:---|---:|

| 4 | **GF** | ~14,000 | Dec 2024 | ~$482,000 | ~$126,000 (R&D ~5,000 est.) | 70.7 | GF 20-F 2024 |

**Peer median headcount-to-300mm-eq-capacity ratio**: ~62.5 (range: 43.3–272.3)

**1σ divergence flagging**: Standard deviation of the ratio set is approximately 76. **Intel (272.3)** is >2.7σ above the median — dramatically more employees per unit of capacity. This reflects Intel's inefficient legacy organizational structure (pre-cost-cutting), its IDM model (design + manufacturing under one roof), and underutilized fab capacity. After the 15% workforce reduction in 2024 (to ~99.5K Intel proper), this ratio should improve in 2025. **Tower Semi (112.0)** is also above 1σ but less extreme given its specialty analog model.

**Sources:** Intel Q4 2024 Earnings Release ([intc.com](https://www.intc.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/1726/intel-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024-financial)), TSMC 2024 Annual Report, GF 20-F, UMC Q4 2024 Results, SMIC 2024 Annual Report, Tower Semiconductor FY2024 Release, Hua Hong 2024 Annual Results.

---

# Q8. Customer Concentration — Reverse-Engineered Identification

| # | Entity | Largest Customer % of FY2024 Revenue | Likely Identity | Confidence | FY2025E Revenue Impact of 30% Pull-in (all else constant) |
|:---|:---|---:|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | **TSMC** | **22%** (disclosed) | **Apple** (confirmed via 20-F: "largest customer accounted for 22% of net revenue in 2024") | **High** — Apple has been TSMC's #1 customer since ~2016; N3/N5 allocation for A18/M4 chips | Revenue impact: −$90.08B × 0.22 × 0.30 = **−$5.95B** |
| 2 | **Samsung Foundry** | **~25-30%** (est.) | **Samsung System LSI (internal)** OR **Qualcomm** (external) | **Medium** — Samsung does not disclose; Qualcomm is the largest external customer (Snapdragon 8 series on SF4); internal SLSI allocation is significant but not a "customer" per se | External revenue impact: −$12.6B × 0.25 × 0.30 = **−$0.95B** |
| 3 | **Intel** | **Not disclosed** (likely Dell/HP/Lenovo ~8-12% each) | **Dell Technologies** (largest OEM partner for Xeon/PC) | **Low** — Intel has highly diversified customer base; no single customer likely exceeds 10% | Impact modest; highly distributed |
| 4 | **GF** | **~15-20%** (est.) | **AMD** (long-term supply agreement through 2026; GF was AMD's former manufacturing arm) | **Medium** — AMD disclosed as >10% customer in GF's S-1; multi-year wafer supply agreement for 12nm/14nm | Revenue impact: −$6.75B × 0.15 × 0.30 = **−$0.30B** |
| 5 | **UMC** | **~12-15%** (est.) | **Qualcomm** or **MediaTek** (22nm RF/WiFi/PMIC) | **Medium** — UMC discloses >10% customers periodically; Qualcomm and MediaTek are the most consistent top-tier foundry partners | Revenue impact: −$7.09B × 0.12 × 0.30 = **−$0.26B** |
| 6 | **SMIC** | **~20-25%** (est.) | **Huawei/HiSilicon** (Kirin 9000S on SMIC N+2) | **Medium-High** — SMIC does not formally disclose but Huawei is widely understood to be the largest customer, especially post-sanctions as the only domestic advanced-node supplier | Revenue impact: −$8.03B × 0.20 × 0.30 = **−$0.48B** |
| 7 | **Tower Semi** | **~12-18%** (est.) | **Intel** (Tower acquired Intel's New Mexico fab in a foundry partnership) or **Broadcom** | **Low** — highly fragmented specialty customer base; no single dominant customer | Revenue impact: −$1.44B × 0.12 × 0.30 = **−$0.05B** |
| 8 | **Hua Hong** | **~18-25%** (est.) | **Chinese state-backed/domestic fabless** (e.g., GigaDevice, Will Semiconductor) | **Low-Medium** — highly domestic China-focused; likely fragmented across Chinese fabless companies | Revenue impact: −$2.00B × 0.18 × 0.30 = **−$0.11B** |

**Methodology and confidence notes:**

- **TSMC**: The 20-F explicitly states "TSMC's largest customer in 2022, 2023 and 2024 accounted for 23%, 25% and 22% of the Company's net revenue." Industry consensus confirms this is Apple. For 2025E, NVIDIA is projected to surpass Apple as #1 customer (~22% vs ~17% per TechPowerUp Feb 2026), but the model here uses 2024 data.

- **Samsung Foundry**: The "largest customer" is ambiguous because Samsung Foundry serves both external customers (Qualcomm, NVIDIA, AMD) and internal Samsung divisions (System LSI for Exynos processors). If treating internal SLSI as a "customer," it likely represents 25-30% of total foundry wafer output. For external-only, Qualcomm is the top external customer.

- **Intel**: Intel's customer base is highly diversified across OEMs, cloud service providers, and distributors. Dell is likely the largest single OEM but well under 10% of consolidated revenue.

- **SMIC-Huawei connection**: Following US sanctions, SMIC became Huawei's primary domestic advanced-node supplier. The Kirin 9000S (Mate 60 Pro) and subsequent Kirin 9010/9020 chips are fabricated on SMIC's N+2 process. While neither party formally discloses the relationship, TechInsights teardown analysis and industry reports make this connection highly probable.

**FY2025E pull-in model**: A 30% pull-in (reduction in orders) by the top customer reduces that customer's contribution by 30%, holding all other revenue constant. This is a simplified partial-equilibrium model; in reality, capacity freed up could be reallocated to other customers with some lag.

**Sources:** TSMC 2024 20-F (customer concentration disclosure), GF S-1/20-F filings, industry reports (TrendForce, Counterpoint, TechInsights, Digitimes), Intel 10-K, SMIC 2024 Annual Report.

| External Revenue | TSMC ($90.1B) | Samsung Foundry ($12.6B) | SMIC ($8.0B) | Tower Semi ($1.4B) |
| Node Leadership | TSMC (N3, score 5) | Samsung (SF4, score 3) | Intel (Intel 3, score 3) | Hua Hong (55nm) |
| CapEx Efficiency | TSMC (1.70) | Tower (0.78) | GF (2.65*) | Intel (0.18) |
| Revenue/Wafer | TSMC ($5,300) | Intel ($3,600) | GF ($3,180) | Hua Hong ($1,110) |
| Gross Margin | TSMC (56.1%) | UMC (32.6%) | Tower (23.6%) | Hua Hong (10.2%) |
| R&D Intensity | Intel (31.2%) | SMIC (10.0%) | Hua Hong (10.0%) | Tower (5.9%) |

*\*GF ranks #3 when measured by capital efficiency ratio [Rev × GM / CapEx], benefiting from extremely low CapEx relative to peers.*

---

**Disclaimer**: Estimates for Samsung Foundry standalone financials are derived from industry analyst reports (TrendForce, Counterpoint, Digitimes) and should be treated as indicative rather than precise, as Samsung does not separately disclose foundry P&L. SMIC and Hua Hong capacity by node classification relies on third-party teardown analysis and may not reflect exact internal allocations. All FX conversions use period-average rates where available and period-end where noted. Data as of most recent annual filings (all FY2024, ended Dec 2024 unless otherwise noted).

Q1.rationale: Pure-play rows are mostly correct, but Samsung relies on analyst consensus without the required DS revenue reconciliation and Intel gives the wrong external revenue/elimination bridge. UMC is capped for using a period-end FX rate despite noting the period-average result.

Q2.rationale: The answer generally identifies the broad node hierarchy, but many maturity scores, lags, and risk/HVM distinctions are incomplete or off. SMIC and Hua Hong are materially wrong on lag or HVM node classification.

Q3.rationale: Most CapEx values are directionally plausible, but the derived WPM ratios are usually off by orders of magnitude and several OCF flags, paybacks, and efficiency ranks are wrong. Intel uses consolidated CapEx without the required foundry allocation.

Q4.rationale: Capacity totals and band splits are mostly inconsistent with the reference, often due to conversion errors or revenue-mix proxies. Intel is especially wrong because the capacity base and revenue-per-wafer miss the intercompany transfer-pricing treatment.

Q5.rationale: Several headline gross margins are correct, but most bridges have wrong signs or magnitudes, especially FX and depreciation. Samsung and Intel do not provide the required segment-level reconstruction with a reconciled bridge.

Q6.rationale: Intel is correctly identified as the main outlier, but many R&D figures or allocations are wrong and the leading-edge R&D-per-kWPM calculations use the wrong scale. UMC is materially off on R&D spending.

Q7.rationale: Some headcounts and revenue-per-employee figures are directionally right, but engineering-headcount denominators and capacity-ratio calculations are often wrong. The sigma flagging misses Samsung and incorrectly flags Tower.

Q8.rationale: The answer frequently uses wrong top-customer shares or identities, and the 30% pull-in sensitivity is modeled with the wrong sign. Intel misses the required intercompany Intel Products customer concentration entirely.

Intel Foundry reports segment operating loss (−$13.4B in FY2024) but does not disclose a standalone foundry gross margin; the massive negative margin reflects intersegment pricing, depreciation on new fabs, and low external volume. Isolating foundry-specific GM for these IDMs requires assumptions about intersegment transfer pricing that are not publicly verifiable.

**IDM R&D Allocation Methodology:**
- **Samsung:** Samsung's DS Division R&D encompasses Memory, System LSI, and Foundry. Samsung does not break out R&D by sub-business. We estimate Foundry R&D at ~60% of the Foundry+System LSI R&D pool (KRW ~7-8T total DS R&D, with Foundry taking a disproportionate share due to 2nm GAA development). **Confidence: Low** — no public split exists.
- **Intel:** Intel's total R&D was $16.5B in FY2024. Intel does not split R&D between Foundry and Products segments in its 10-K. We estimate ~55% allocated to Foundry (process technology development, manufacturing R&D) based on the foundry headcount share and the intensity of process technology investment. **Confidence: Low** — no public split exists.

**R&D-per-Leading-Edge-Wafer Ranking (for firms with ≤7nm capacity):**
1. Samsung Foundry: ~$5,745 (highest intensity, but smallest LE capacity base)
2. TSMC: ~$1,717

**Outlier Identification:** **Samsung Foundry** is the outlier whose R&D intensity (~35% of foundry revenue) is most disconnected from its node-leadership rank (#2 in HVM leading node, but spending at a rate that implies #1 ambition). **Flagged Divergences:**
- **Intel Foundry** (112.5): >1σ above median. Intel's foundry headcount is inflated relative to its external output because the vast majority of its manufacturing serves internal Intel Products. The headcount-to-capacity ratio reflects an IDM structure, not a pure-play foundry.
- **Hua Hong** (411 on 8"-eq basis; ~57 when converted to 12"-eq): When properly normalized to 300mm-equivalent capacity, Hua Hong is near the median. The apparent divergence on an 8"-eq basis reflects its small-diameter wafer production, not true inefficiency.

## Q8. Customer Concentration — Reverse-Engineered Identification

| Entity | Largest Customer % of FY2024 Rev | Likely Identity | Confidence | Top-10 % | FY2025E Impact of 30% Top-Customer Pull-in (USD M) |
|--------|----------------------------------|-----------------|------------|----------|---------------------------------------------------|
| TSMC | **22%** (disclosed) | Apple | **High** | ~76% | 90,080 × 0.22 × 0.30 = **+5,945** |
| Samsung Foundry | **~40%** (est.) | Qualcomm | **Medium** | ~85% (est.) | 7,760 × 0.40 × 0.30 = **+931** |
| Intel Foundry | **~85%** (captive) | Intel Products (internal) | **High** | N/A (captive-dominated) | 328 × 0.85 × 0.30 = **+84** |
| GlobalFoundries | **~15%** (est.) | AMD / Qualcomm / Broadcom | **Medium** | ~55% | 6,750 × 0.15 × 0.30 = **+304** |
| UMC | **~20%** (est.) | Qualcomm / MediaTek | **Medium** | ~60% | 7,225 × 0.20 × 0.30 = **+434** |
| SMIC | **~25%** (est.) | HiSilicon (Huawei) / Chinese fabless | **Medium** | ~75% | 8,030 × 0.25 × 0.30 = **+602** |

| Hua Hong | **~20%** (est.) | Chinese fabless (e.g., Will Semiconductor) | **Low** | ~65% | 2,004 × 0.20 × 0.30 = **+120** |

**Detailed Customer Identification:**

- **TSMC:** Per the 2024 Annual Report and 20-F, the largest customer accounted for **22%** of net revenue (down from 25% in 2023 and 23% in 2022). This is **Apple** (high confidence — widely known as TSMC's largest customer for A-series/M-series chips). The second-largest customer accounted for **12%** (likely **NVIDIA**, given surging AI chip demand; NVIDIA's TSMC revenue share grew from ~6% in 2023 to ~12% in 2024 per analyst estimates). Top-10 customers comprised ~76% of revenue.

- **Samsung Foundry:** Samsung does not disclose foundry customer concentration. **Qualcomm** is widely reported as Samsung's largest external foundry customer (Snapdragon SoCs on SF4/SF4P). Internal System LSI (Exynos) represents a major "captive" customer. External concentration is estimated at ~40% for the largest customer. **Confidence: Medium.**

- **Intel Foundry:** The dominant "customer" is **Intel Products** (CCG + DCAI + NEX), representing ~98% of Intel Foundry's segment revenue ($17.2B of $17.5B). External customers contributed only ~$328M. This is a captive-dominated foundry with minimal external diversification. **Confidence: High** for internal; **Low** for external customer identity.

- **GlobalFoundries:** GF's customer base is relatively diversified across automotive, aerospace/defense, IoT, and mobile. No single customer exceeds 15% per historical disclosures. AMD remains a significant customer on 12nm/14nm. **Confidence: Medium.**

- **SMIC:** SMIC disclosed that revenue from Chinese customers increased YoY and constituted the vast majority of revenue (per FY2024 annual report). **HiSilicon** (Huawei) is widely believed to be the largest customer, though not confirmed by SMIC. **Confidence: Medium** for identity.

- **Hua Hong:** Serves primarily Chinese domestic customers in power management, MCU, and analog. **Will Semiconductor** (韦尔股份) is reported as a major customer. **Confidence: Low** — Hua Hong does not disclose individual customer concentrations.

**FY2025E Revenue Impact Model:** A 30% pull-in (order acceleration) by each firm's top customer, holding all other revenue constant, would add the amounts shown in the rightmost column. TSMC benefits most in absolute terms (+$5.9B) due to its scale, while Intel Foundry benefits least (+$84M) due to its minimal external revenue base.

Q1.rationale: Pure-play foundry rows were mostly accurate, but the two key intercompany-elimination traps were badly missed: Samsung external revenue was far too low and Intel used an incorrect intersegment elimination. UMC was numerically correct but lacked the expected filing-level support.

Q2.rationale: The answer captured some broad node hierarchy but often missed the exact HVM-vs-risk distinction, maturity scores, lag baseline, or fab/source specificity. Intel, SMIC, Tower, and Hua Hong were materially wrong on leading-node characterization.

Q3.rationale: Most CapEx headline values were directionally plausible, but the derived ratios, paybacks, WPM denominators, and efficiency rankings were frequently wrong. Intel and Samsung also used distorted revenue bases or weak allocation logic.

Q4.rationale: TSMC was partly correct, but most capacity totals and band splits were substantially off, especially for Intel, SMIC, Hua Hong, and GlobalFoundries. Several rows failed the 300mm-equivalent conversion or leading-edge capacity caveats.

Q5.rationale: Only GlobalFoundries had a reasonably tied gross-margin bridge. Most rows had wrong component signs or magnitudes, missing normalized margins, or no segment reconstruction for Samsung and Intel.

Q6.rationale: The answer missed the required leading-edge intensity ranking and incorrectly identified Samsung rather than Intel as the main outlier. Several R&D values, denominators, and per-kWPM units were wrong or omitted.

Q7.rationale: Headcount values were often directionally plausible, but engineering-headcount denominators, CapEx-per-engineer, capacity ratios, and sigma flags were largely incorrect. Samsung and Intel ND handling was weak.

Q8.rationale: The answer attempted identities and pull-in math, but most customer percentages were materially wrong and several rows asserted >10% customers where filings indicate none. Intel’s intercompany pull-in sensitivity was also scaled to the wrong revenue base.

1. **Samsung Foundry:** No separate foundry revenue disclosure; DS Division consolidates Memory, System LSI, and Foundry

Q1.rationale: Pure-play rows were often directionally correct but lacked specific citations and used wrong FX conventions for TSMC/UMC/SMIC. Samsung and Intel failed the central intercompany-elimination figures by large margins.

Q2.rationale: Several rows identified broad node positioning, but Intel, UMC, Tower, and Hua Hong used wrong leading HVM nodes or lag estimates. Citations and risk-vs-HVM distinctions were generally weak.

Q3.rationale: CapEx values and capital-efficiency rankings were largely wrong, including unallocated Samsung DS capex and materially overstated TSMC capex. Multiple OCF flags and payback calculations were incorrect.

Q4.rationale: Capacity figures were mostly off by factors due to annual/monthly and 8-inch/300mm-equivalent confusion. Some directional node-band classifications were present, but revenue-per-wafer and utilization classifications were often wrong.

Q5.rationale: Only Hua Hong substantially captured the magnitude and depreciation driver. Most other bridges had wrong component signs, wrong GM deltas, missing segment reconstruction, or non-reconciling attribution.

Q6.rationale: R&D values and per-leading-edge-capacity ratios were mostly incorrect, with several pure-play R&D figures far outside tolerance. Intel was identified as an outlier, but the required ranking and allocation methodology were not correctly executed.

Q7.rationale: Some headcounts were directionally close, but engineering-headcount denominators, capacity ratios, and sigma flags were mostly wrong or unit-inconsistent. Samsung was not properly apportioned to foundry-only headcount.

Q8.rationale: The answer named several plausible customers, but many concentration percentages were outside bands and the 30% pull-in impacts were frequently wrong in sign and scale. Intel correctly identified intercompany dominance but missed the consolidated-elimination caveat.

| # | Entity | Top-1 Customer % FY2024 | Top-10 % FY2024 | Likely Top-1 Identity | Confidence | FY2025E Rev Impact of 30% Pull-in by Top Customer (USD M) |

| 1 | TSMC | **22%** | ~78% | **Apple** (A-series/M-series SoCs) | **High** | +$5,940M (Apple = 22% of $90.08B × 30%) |
| 2 | Samsung Foundry | Est. ~25–30% | N/A | **Samsung System LSI** (Exynos) + Qualcomm | **Medium** | +$945M (est. 25% of $12.6B × 30%) |

**Reverse-Engineering Notes**:
- **TSMC**: Annual Report 2024 explicitly states: "Our largest customer in 2022, 2023 and 2024 accounted for 23%, 25% and 22% of our net revenue." Industry consensus identifies this as Apple (A-series/M-series). Confidence: **High**.
- **GlobalFoundries**: 20-F states top 10 customers accounted for ~65% of revenue. Historical filings identified AMD (~21%) and Qualcomm (~11%) in 2020; post-LTA restructuring, AMD remains largest. Confidence: **Medium**.
- **Samsung Foundry**: Largest customer is likely Samsung's own System LSI division (internal intercompany), with Qualcomm as the largest external customer. **Not separately disclosed**. Confidence: **Medium**.
- **SMIC**: Huawei/HiSilicon is widely reported as the dominant customer for 7nm-capable Chinese foundry services. SMIC does not disclose individual customer percentages. Confidence: **Medium**.
- **UMC, Tower, Hua Hong**: No individual customer exceeds 10% disclosure threshold in public filings. Top customers inferred from known design-win relationships (MediaTek for UMC DDI; ST/onsemi for Tower; Will Semi/GalaxyCore for Hua Hong CIS). Confidence: **Low**.

**FY2025E Revenue Impact Model**: Assuming a 30% pull-in (reduction) by the single largest customer, holding all other revenue constant:
- TSMC faces the largest absolute risk ($5.9B impact).
- Intel Foundry external revenue impact is minimal ($96M) because external revenue is already near-zero.
- Pure-play foundries with diversified customer bases (GF, UMC, Tower) show moderate single-customer risk.

Samsung Foundry's ~$12.6B revenue is an analyst/TrendForce estimate, not a company disclosure. Intel Foundry's $328M external revenue is derived from segment-level elimination but may include minor external ASIC/services revenue. Capacity figures for Samsung, Intel, and Tower are industry estimates rather than disclosed numbers. All values should be treated as best-available approximations based on public filings and credible third-party sources.

Q1.rationale: Pure-play rows were mostly correct, but Samsung relied on analyst estimates without DS residual reconciliation and Intel used an incorrect intersegment elimination, materially understating external revenue.

Q2.rationale: The answer repeatedly misclassified risk or early-ramp nodes as HVM, especially TSMC N2, Intel 18A, and SMIC N+2. Specialty/mature-node firms were handled better, but lags and risk-node distinctions were often wrong.

Q3.rationale: CapEx headline values were sometimes close, but the required ratio decomposition was largely wrong, especially CapEx per incremental WPM and payback. Samsung and Intel failed the required foundry allocation methodology.

Q4.rationale: Most total capacity and band splits were materially wrong, including severe 200mm-to-300mm conversion errors and incorrect leading-edge shares. Some classifications and as-of dates were directionally present, supporting only minimal credit.

Q5.rationale: GlobalFoundries was well reconciled, and SMIC/Hua Hong had partial bridge logic, but several entities had wrong GM levels or component signs. Samsung and Intel lacked the required quantified segment bridge.

Q7.rationale: Several headcounts were directionally plausible, but engineering-headcount denominators, CapEx-per-engineer, and headcount-to-capacity ratios were mostly mis-scaled. Samsung lacked a foundry apportionment and Hua Hong used an unsupported estimate.

Q8.rationale: The answer often missed disclosed customer concentration percentages or named the wrong likely customer, especially GF, Tower, and SMIC. UMC received partial credit for correctly treating the top customer as below 10% and estimating a pull-in impact.

## Sources & Methodology Note
Data drawn from official FY2024 annual reports, 20-F/10-K filings, earnings releases, and investor presentations. FX rates used (period-average unless noted): **TWD/USD ≈ 31.5** (TSMC, UMC), **KRW/USD ≈ 1,350** (Samsung), **HKD/USD ≈ 7.79** (SMIC, Hua Hong), **USD as-reported** (GF, Intel, Tower). TSMC FY2024 consolidated revenue of NT$2,894.31B = **US$90.08B** (disclosed). All figures USD millions unless noted.

---

## Q1. External Foundry Revenue — Intercompany Elimination

| # | Entity | Consolidated Revenue | Intercompany Elimination | External Foundry Revenue | FX Rate Used |
|---|--------|---------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------|-------------|
| 1 | **TSMC (TSM)** | $90,080M | None (pure-play) | **$90,080M** | NT$31.5/USD avg |
| 2 | **Samsung Foundry** | ~$13,700M est. (DS segment non-memory) | ~$4,500M (→ System LSI) | **~$9,200M** | KRW 1,350/USD |
| 3 | **Intel Foundry** | $17,500M (segment) | $17,200M (→ Intel Products) | **~$300M external** | USD |
| 4 | **GlobalFoundries (GFS)** | $6,750M | None (pure-play) | **$6,750M** | USD |
| 5 | **UMC** | $7,085M (~$229.1B TWD @ 31.5) | None (single segment) | **$7,085M** | NT$31.5/USD avg |
| 6 | **SMIC (0981.HK)** | $8,030M | None (standalone) | **$8,030M** | RMB 7.2/USD avg |
| 7 | **Tower Semiconductor (TSEM)** | $1,436M | None (single segment) | **$1,436M** | USD |
| 8 | **Hua Hong (1347.HK)** | $2,004M | None (standalone) | **$2,004M** | RMB 7.2/USD avg |

### Key Eliminations

- **TSMC**: Pure-play foundry; no intercompany elimination required. External revenue = consolidated revenue.
- **Samsung Foundry**: DS non-memory sales of ~KRW 18.5T (~$13.7B) include both Foundry (external customers) and System LSI (captive). Captive wafer transfers to System LSI estimated at ~$4.5B based on System LSI revenue of ~$5.5B. External foundry revenue = **~$9.2B** (per Counterpoint ~8% pure-play market share × ~$131.7B industry = ~$10.5B → revised to ~$9.2B per TechInAsia). *Limitation: Samsung does not separately disclose foundry vs. System LSI in K-IFRS; figure is analyst-estimated.*
- **Intel Foundry**: Segment revenue $17.5B (GAAP) includes ~$17.2B intersegment (Intel Products insourcing). External revenue = **~$300M** (per LinkedIn analysis of 10-Q filings: ~$53M per half-year external). *Limitation: Intel's "internal foundry" model means most segment revenue is cost-plus intersegment; external third-party revenue is minimal.*
- **GF / UMC / SMIC / Tower / Hua Hong**: Pure-play or standalone; no material intercompany elimination.
- **Hua Hong**: Single segment; $2,004M full-year revenue confirmed in Q4 2024 earnings release.

---

## Q2. Process Node Maturity — Risk vs. HVM Distinction

**HVM Definition**: ≥10,000 WPM sustained for ≥2 consecutive quarters as of Q1 2026.

| # | Entity | Smallest HVM Node | Score (1–5) | HVM Fab Location | Risk Production Nodes | Lag vs. TSMC HVM Leading |
|---|--------|-------------------|-------------|------------------|----------------------|-------------------------|
| 1 | **TSMC** | **N2** (2nm, volume production Q4 2025) | **5** | Taiwan (Fab 20 P8), Arizona (Fab 21) | A14 (development) | Leader |
| 2 | **Samsung Foundry** | **SF3 (3nm-class, 3GAP)** in volume production H2 2024 | **3** | Giheung, Hwaseong (Korea) | SF2 (2nm) in risk production (DK released) | **~2 years** |
| 3 | **Intel Foundry** | **Intel 3** (in HVM ramp 2024); Intel 18A (initial production, Panther Lake tape-out Dec 2024) | **2** | Oregon (D1X), Arizona (Fab 52/62) | Intel 14A (risk) | **~3 years** |
| 4 | **GlobalFoundries** | **12nm (12LP+)** — mature specialty node; no EUV leading edge | **4** | Malta (NY), Singapore, Dresden | N/A (14nm and above) | N/A (mature node strategy) |
| 5 | **UMC** | **22nm** — specialty nodes (22nm ULP, 28nm) | **4** | Taiwan (Fab 8A/12A) | N/A (not pursuing leading edge) | N/A |
| 6 | **SMIC** | **28nm** — N+2 (equivalent 7nm, limited HVM); primary HVM is 28nm | **2** | Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen | N+2 (DUV-based ~7nm, limited volume) | **~5 years** |
| 7 | **Tower Semiconductor** | **SiGe, BiCMOS, 65nm** — analog/mixed-signal specialty | **3** | Israel (Migdal Ha'emek), US, Japan (TPSCo) | 300mm Agrate (Intel partnership, 65nm) | N/A (differentiated specialty) |
| 8 | **Hua Hong** | **55nm specialty** — 12" fabs Wuxi (90k wpm); 8" legacy | **3** | Shanghai (Jinqiao/Zhangjiang), Wuxi | N/A (specialty focus) | N/A |

### Maturity Scoring Key
- **5** = High-yield HVM at most advanced node, ≥2 consecutive quarters
- **4** = Mature HVM node, stable yield, volume production
- **3** = Ramping HVM with improving yield; risk production co-existing
- **2** = Early-stage HVM or limited-volume production
- **1** = R&D / pre-production only

### Node-Lag Commentary
- **TSMC N2** entered HVM Q4 2025; **Samsung SF2** is risk production (DK released, volume target 2025–2026).
- **Intel 18A** achieved first customer tape-out (Panther Lake) but full HVM not yet confirmed at ≥10k WPM as of Q1 2026.
- **SMIC N+2** uses DUV multi-patterning for ~7nm equivalent; yield rates estimated at 60–70% vs. TSMC's 90%+.
